newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Hardliners delay bill, Belgrade students rally.
newsitem.headline: Hardliners delay bill, Belgrade students rally.

text.p: Serbian ultra-nationalists on Tuesday delayed parliament's vote on reinstating opposition victories in local elections while students launched a new round of pro-democracy street protests.

Reporters outside parliament were able to watch closed-circuit television showing 147 parliamentarians gather in the 250-seat assembly. It quickly became apparent that the Radicals, an ultra-nationalist party with 35 parliamentarians, were holding up the legislation.
"Absolutely there was an obstruction of parliament by the Radical Party," federal trade minister Djordje Siradovic told reporters. "I don't understand what they are really after."

Milosevic's Socialists had annulled November's opposition victories in 14 towns and cities including Belgrade on grounds of "irregularities". The action prompted three months of huge protests and attracted an international outcry.
A week ago Milosevic suddenly announced he was asking parliament to approve a bill recognising the opposition gains.

The three-party opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition saw Milosevic's introduction of a "lex specialis" or special law as a climbdown and a triumphal outcome of huge protests in Belgrade and other cities.
But suspecting subterfuge on the part of the Socialists, opposition politicians say they plan to keep up the pressure by continuing the street rallies.

"We are facing a long hot spring and summer and a fight against those who have not surrendered, those who regard their own people as a foreign element," opposition leader Zoran Djindjic told thousands of supporters in Belgrade on Monday.

Zajedno has said it fears that even when the special bill is passed by parliament, Milosevic will remove the already limited powers of local councils with legislation stripping them of their sources of revenue.

In Washington, U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright issued a personal appeal to Milosevic, urging him to ensure the disputed election results were reinstated and to open a dialogue with his opponents.
Her comments were contained in a letter delivered to Milosevic on Saturday.

The United States remained sceptical that Milosevic would honour his pledge to recognise the poll results and Albright felt she should write to him personally to let him know "the strong concern of the United States on these issues," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said.
Tuesday's draft bill recognising the disputed November 17 election results was fourth on the list of parliamentary items.
"You will hear a lot from the Radicals during this session," Radical parliamentary leader Tomislav Nikolic told the MPs.
A government reshuffle is also on the day's agenda.
The Radicals have submitted draft amendments challenging the election bill, saying that as it stands it allows the international community to use parliament to legalise decrees imposed from above.
Milosevic's Socialists have 123 parliamentarians, but they have usually managed to get their way with the support of ethnic minority representatives.

During Tuesday's debate, Serbian Prime Minister and Milosevic stalwart Mirko Marjanovic said "clever media manipulators" had used the protests to portray Serbia as unstable, resulting in a deterioration of the country's reputation.
"By voting for this (election) law, you will confirm that the interests of the state and citizens must always be above narrow party interests," he said.
In bright sunlight, meanwhile, thousands of students began the day's round of protest marches with an eight (five-mile) walk through downtown Belgrade.
A student organiser said they planned to carry in the vanguard two large lifebelts, made of ice, as an offering to the ruling Socialists "to bail themselves out".
